messages.content: "In a physics experiment, you are given two charges. The first charge has a magnitude of 5 coulombs and the second charge has a magnitude of 10 coulombs. These charges are placed at a distance of 2 meters from each other. You are asked to calculate the electromagnetic force between these charges. You perform the experiment twice. The first time, the charges are placed in a vacuum, which has a permittivity of 8.854 x 10^-12 F/m. The second time, the charges are placed in a medium with a relative permittivity of 5 x 10^-12 F/m. Can you calculate the electromagnetic force between the charges in both scenarios?"

function.name: electromagnetic_force
function.description: Calculate the electromagnetic force between two charges placed at a certain distance. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

charge1.description: The magnitude of the first charge in coulombs.

charge2.description: The magnitude of the second charge in coulombs.

distance.description: The distance between the two charges in meters.

medium_permittivity.description: The relative permittivity of the medium in which the charges are present. Default is 8.854 x 10^-12 F/m (vacuum permittivity). This is a float type value.

message.content:
**Coulomb’s law**

\[
F=\frac{q_1\,q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon\,r^{2}}
\]

where  

* \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) are the magnitudes of the charges (Coulombs)  
* \(r\) is the separation (meters)  
* \(\varepsilon\) is the absolute permittivity of the medium (Farads / meter)  

The constant \(k = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon}\) is often written as \(k = 8.987551787\times10^{9}\;\text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2\) when \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0=8.854\times10^{-12}\;\text{F/m}\).

---

### 1.  Vacuum

* \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0 = 8.854\times10^{-12}\;\text{F/m}\)  
* \(q_1 = 5\;\text{C}\)  
* \(q_2 = 10\;\text{C}\)  
* \(r = 2\;\text{m}\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
k_{\text{vac}} &= \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}
                = 8.987551787\times10^{9}\;\text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2 \\[4pt]
F_{\text{vac}} &= k_{\text{vac}}\;\frac{q_1q_2}{r^2}
                = 8.987551787\times10^{9}\;\frac{5\times10}{(2)^2} \\[4pt]
                &= 8.987551787\times10^{9}\;\frac{50}{4}
                = 8.987551787\times10^{9}\times12.5 \\[4pt]
                &= 1.12344\times10^{11}\;\text{N}
\end{aligned}
\]

**Result (vacuum):**  
\[
\boxed{F_{\text{vac}} \approx 1.12\times10^{11}\ \text{N}}
\]

---

### 2.  Medium with \(\varepsilon = 5\times10^{-12}\;\text{F/m}\)

(Here the problem gives an *absolute* permittivity of \(5\times10^{-12}\;\text{F/m}\).)

\[
\begin{aligned}
k_{\text{med}} &= \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{\text{med}}}
                = \frac{1}{4\pi(5\times10^{-12})}
                = 1.591549431\times10^{10}\;\text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2 \\[4pt]
F_{\text{med}} &= k_{\text{med}}\;\frac{q_1q_2}{r^2}
                = 1.591549431\times10^{10}\;\frac{50}{4} \\[4pt]
                &= 1.591549431\times10^{10}\times12.5 \\[4pt]
                &= 1.98944\times10^{11}\;\text{N}
\end{aligned}
\]

**Result (medium):**  
\[
\boxed{F_{\text{med}} \approx 1.99\times10^{11}\ \text{N}}
\]

---

### Summary

| Medium | Permittivity \(\varepsilon\) (F/m) | Force \(F\) (N) |
|--------|-----------------------------------|-----------------|
| Vacuum | \(8.854\times10^{-12}\) | \(1.12\times10^{11}\) |
| Medium | \(5\times10^{-12}\) | \(1.99\times10^{11}\) |

Because both charges are positive, the force is **repulsive** in both cases. The larger force in the medium arises from its lower permittivity, which reduces the “screening” effect and allows the electric field to be stronger.
